Up until now, we have learned how to import data from various sources
into our `R` session in the form of tables called "`tibbles`". To gain
better insight, we need tools to *manipulate* the data.

![](illustrations/fig-data-wrangling.png)

Several packages allow us to perform these tasks. In this unit, we will
talk about some tools included in `{dplyr}`, `{janitor}` and `{tidyr}`

# A Grammar for Data Manipulation {#DataManip}

```{r ,echo = FALSE, fig.cap='The pliers of `{dplyr}` will help us wrangle our data!', fig.align='center', out.width = "30%"}
  knitr::include_graphics(
    path = str_glue("https://d33wubrfki0l68.cloudfront.net/\\
                    621a9c8c5d7b47c4b6d72e8f01f28d14310e8370\\
                    /193fc/css/images/hex/\\
                    dplyr.png")
    )
```

The package `{dplyr}` offers a series of functions or *verbs* that help
us **wrangle** data the same way we use a plier to wrangle wires. Some
of the *verbs* contained in `{dplyr}` are:

|           Verb            | Use                                                                                                 |
|:------------------------------:|---------------------------------------|
|        `select()`         | **pick a set of columns** from a `tibble`                                                           |
|        `filter()`         | **pick a set of rows**                                                                              |
|        `mutate()`         | **transform and add columns** to the `tibble`                                                       |
|        `arrange()`        | **order the rows** according to the values of a (set of) column(s)                                  |
|       `group_by()`        | **group** according to the values of a (set of) column(s) to perform calculations within the groups |
| `summarise()/summarize()` | to create a new `tibble` containing **summary statistics** for a set of columns                     |

::: blackbox
**Remark:** These functions are called *verbs* because, thanks to the
**pipe** operator, they can be **written sequentially**, since:

Their **first argument** is the **name of the dataset**

The **remaining arguments** are the **names of the columns**

For example:

``` r
select(dataset, column_1, column_2)

# Is equivalent to:

dataset %>% select(column_1, column_2)

# you see that it reads like a sentence!
```
:::

## Inspecting Data

For the illustrations, we will rely on the WTA dataset that you can
import with `read_csv()` (with extra arguments to avoid importing
errors).

```{r}
library(readr)

wta_data <-
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gruggeri/tennis_wta/master/wta_grand_slam_data.csv" %>% 
  read_csv(
    # setting the argument `col_types = cols(.default = "c")` 
    # where `"c"` stands for `character`. 
    col_types = cols(.default = "c")
    # This is because `read_csv` "guesses" the type of each column (numeric, 
    # character, etc.) by parsing the first 10000 lines. 
    # Since we have a lot of missing observations in some columns, this could  
    # yield importing errors
    ) 
```

We can print a summary of the contents using the function `glimpse()`.

```{r, eval = TRUE}
glimpse(wta_data)
```

As you can see, the dataset contains many columns, most of them prefixed
with a descriptive enough prefix. Here's a breakdown of the most
important, i.e. those we'll use in what follows.

| column / prefix | Content                                                                        |
|:-----------------------------------:|:----------------------------------|
|     `year`      | Year of the tournament the match took place                                    |
|   `tourney_*`   | Information related to the tournament (`id`, `name`, `surface`, ...)           |
|   `match_num`   | Number of match **within a tournament**                                        |
|   `winner_*`    | Information related to the winner of a given match (`id`, `name`, `hand`, ...) |
|    `loser_*`    | Information related to the loser of a given match (`id`, `name`, `hand`, ...)  |

Alternatively, we can have a *graphical* view, using the function
`vis_dat()` from the package `{visdat}`, which gives us an overview of
the dataset's contents.

-   The colors display the `types` of the columns (character, numeric,
    date... )
-   The gray denotes missing observations.

```{r,  echo = TRUE, fig.cap = "A bird's-eye view of the WTA dataset using `vis_dat()`"}
library(visdat)
wta_data %>% 
  vis_dat(
    # `warn_large_data = FALSE` added to avoid warnings
    warn_large_data = FALSE
    )  
```

## `select()`

The function `select()` helps **picking column**. For instance, we can
**pick a column by its name**, such as the column `year`, as in:

```{r, eval = FALSE,  out.width ="80%"}
wta_data %>% 
  select(year)
```

We can select more than one column, and for that, we add their names in
our call to `select()`. Say, we want to select information related to
the **winners** and the **tourneys**, we can do that by adding the names
of those columns:

```{r, eval = FALSE,  out.width ="80%"}
wta_data %>% 
  select(year,tourney_id, tourney_name, winner_id, winner_name)
```

`{dplyr}` also understands how to **pick columns using conditions on the
column names** by means of **selection helpers**. For instance, let's
use `starts_with()` to pick all the columns that **start with** the
aforementioned prefixes `tourney_` and `winner_`. To make things even
clearer, let's inspect the result with `vis_dat()`!

```{r,  out.width ="80%", out.height="80%"}
wta_data %>% 
  select(year, starts_with("winner"), starts_with("tourney")) %>% 
  vis_dat(warn_large_data = FALSE)
```

Most of the other selection helpers have almost self-explanatory names,
e.g.

| Selection Helper | Case use                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|:-----------------------------------------:|:----------------------------|
|  `ends_with()`   | selects according to a suffix                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|   `contains()`   | when we are looking for columns that contain a literal word or string                                                                                                                                                        |
|   `matches()`    | selects according to **patterns known as Regular expressions**. Some of the most essentials are described in the [cheatsheet of the package `{stringr}`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/regex.html) |
|  `num_range()`   | which helps selecting columns that have numbers, e.g. `x01`, `x02`, ... we're interested in a range, e.g. `num_range("x", 10:15)`                                                                                            |

Other selection helpers apply to column names, such as `all_of()`
`any_of()` and finally `where()` which selects according to functions.

## `mutate()`

The `mutate()` verb allows us to **create new columns** or **transform
existing ones**.

For instance, at the beginning of this unit, we imported all columns
into our session as `character`, but **`year` should be numerical** and
**`tourney_date` should be dates**.

We change the column type with `mutate()`, `as.numeric()` and `ymd()`
from the package `{lubridate}`, as in:

```{r,  out.width ="80%"}
library(lubridate)

wta_data <- 
  wta_data %>% 
  mutate(
    year = as.numeric(year),
    tourney_date = ymd(tourney_date))
  
wta_data %>% 
  select(year, starts_with("winner"), starts_with("tourney")) %>%  
  vis_dat(warn_large_data = FALSE)
```

In the plot, we see that the `Type` of the column `year` has switched
from `character` to `numeric`, and column `tourney_date` has changed to
`Date`.

Notice that **to make these changes permanent**, we have *assigned* the
last data pipe into `wta_data`, thereby **rewriting the tibble**.

## `filter()`

We use the `filter()` function to **create subsets of a tibble according
to logical conditions**. These logical conditions apply to the values
contained in a column and will **pick the rows fulfilling the
condition**.

-   Here's a quick rundown on how to write logical conditions in R

|       Logical Condition        |  Symbol  |
|:------------------------------:|:--------:|
|         *A equal to B*         | `A == B` |
|        *A less than B*         | `A < B`  |
| *A less than or equal to to B* | `A <= B` |
|       *A greater than B*       | `A > B`  |
|   *A greater or equal to B*    | `A >= B` |

-   One can also combine conditions, as in :

|       Logical Condition       |          Syntax           |
|:-----------------------------:|:-------------------------:|
| *Condition 1 AND Condition 2* | `ConditionA & ConditionB` |
| *Condition 1 OR Condition 2*  | `ConditionA | ConditionB` |

-   Finally, a very handy shortcut for multiple `OR` conditions is the
    `%in%` operator, which compares a value to the contents of a vector!
    For instance:

```{=html}
<!-- -->
```
    A == B | A == C | A == C  

is equivalent to:

    A %in% c(B, C, D)

Say, for instance, that we are interested in analysing the career of the
great Serena Williams. We can start our analysis by filtering the
matches she won using the condition `winner_name == 'Serena Williams'`.
This yields the following tibble:

```{r,  out.width ="80%"}
wta_data %>% 
  select(year, starts_with("winner"), starts_with("tourney")) %>% 
  filter(winner_name == "Serena Williams")
```

We could also add other conditions. Let's suppose we are interested in
analysing her performance at the Australian tournaments, we could select
all the instances where `tourney_name` contains the pattern `Australian`
with `str_detect()` from the package `{stringr}`, a function that
detects when the `tourney_name` contains the pattern "Australian".

```{r}
library(stringr)
wta_data %>%
  filter(
    winner_name == "Serena Williams", 
    str_detect(tourney_name, pattern = "Australian")) # str_detect returns TRUE if `tourney_name` contains the pattern "Australian"
```

## `arrange()`

The verb `arrange()` allows you to **order observations** according to
the values of columns of your dataset.

-   If the ordering column is of **type `numeric`**, naturally, they
    will be ordered in **increasing order of the numbers**

```{r}
wta_data %>%
  select(year,  winner_name, tourney_name) %>% 
  arrange(year)
```

-   If the ordering column is of **type `character`**, the observations
    will be arranged in alphabetic order.

```{r}
wta_data %>%
  select(year, winner_name, tourney_name) %>% 
  arrange(winner_name)
```

Moreover, you can order your observations according to more than one
column.

-   The order in which you introduce this into `arrange()` is important.
    `{dplyr}` will order **first** according to the name of the column
    you introduce first and then, by the second:

```{r}
wta_data %>%
  select(year, winner_name, tourney_name) %>% 
  arrange(year, winner_name)
```

By default, **`arrange()` sorts observations in *ascending* order**.

-   We can order in *descending* order by enclosing the ordering column
    with the argument `desc()`

```{r}
wta_data %>%
  select(year, winner_name, tourney_name) %>% 
  arrange(year, desc(winner_name))
```

## `summarise()`

The function `summarise()` creates a new dataset that **contains
summaries of the required columns**.

Let's say that we are interested in the number of matches won by Serena
Williams in the Australian tournaments. Once subsetted with `filter()`,
we can count the number of matches with the helper function `n()`, which
**computes the number of rows** as in:

```{r,  out.width ="80%"}
wta_data %>%
  filter(
    winner_name == "Serena Williams", 
    str_detect(tourney_name, pattern = "Australian")) %>% 
  summarise(number_of_wins = n())
```

Aside from `n()`, other useful functions can calculate various other
summaries.

| Summary Statistic | Functions                      |
|:-----------------:|:-------------------------------|
|      Center       | `mean()`, `median()`           |
|      Spread       | `sd()`, `IQR()`, `mad()`       |
|       Range       | `min()`, `max()`, `quantile()` |
|     Position      | `first()`, `last()`, `nth()`   |
|       Count       | `n()`, `n_distinct()`          |
|      Logical      | `any()`, `all()`               |

## `group_by()`

Some analyses require that we **group the data** according to **single
or multiple *grouping* factors** before performing calculations. This
can be achieved using `group_by()`.

For instance, let's group the dataset by `winner_name`:

```{r}
wta_data %>%
  group_by(winner_name)
```

You might think this operation does not change anything substantial in
the dataset. However, notice that **the output in the console (or the
preview) reveals the grouping column**. This implies that from now on,
**all computations will be done within the groups defined by the column
values**.

To remove a grouping structure, use the verb `ungroup()`:

```{r}
wta_data %>%
  group_by(winner_name) %>% 
  ungroup()
```

## `group_by()` `%>%` `summarise()`

As we said previously, **the call to `group_by()` implies that all the
manipulations that come afterwards will be carried in the groups**.

This ties neatly with `summarise()`, creating **summary statistics for
the groups** defined by the different values of the column!

Let's illustrate its use by counting the number of wins of every player
listed in the dataset. After a call to group by, **`n()` will count the
rows within the groups created by the values of the column**, in this
case, the number of times each `winner_name` appears in the dataset.

```{r}
wta_data %>%
  group_by(winner_name)%>% 
  summarise(number_of_wins = n()) %>% 
  ungroup()
```

-   Moreover, we can group via more than one column.

Let's use this function to see **how many matches** were won by **each
player** in **each tournament**. For this, we need to
`group_by(winner_name, tourney_name)`:

```{r}
wta_data %>%
  group_by(winner_name, tourney_name)%>% 
  summarise(number_of_wins = n()) %>% 
  ungroup()
```

# Merging Data

In real situations, information can be stored not in only one, but in a
series of datasets. To have a single tibble that contains all the
information we need, we would to combine, or *merge* `tibbles` with the
help of `{dplyr}` *verbs*. The most important are the *binding* verbs
and the *join* verbs.

|     Verb      | Use                                                                          |
|:------------------------------:|---------------------------------------|
| `bind_rows()` | merges two tibbles by **stacking them up** (one on top of the other)         |
| `bind_cols()` | merges two tibbles by **attaching them** (one next to the other)             |
|  `*_join()`   | **attaches** tibbles by **the columns they have in common** (joining *keys*) |

Let's create two simple examples that allow us to understand this logic.
The following code generates some tibbles, endowed with an `id` a series
of columns, `var_1`, `var_2`, `var_3`

```{r}
data_1 <- tibble(id = 1:3, var_1 = c(15, 13, 39))
data_2 <- tibble(id = c(4, 5), var_1 = 10)
data_3<- tibble(id = 1:3, var_2 = c(10, 12,14), var_3 = c(45,20, 2)) 
```

Let's print them to see their contents

```{r}
data_1
```

```{r}
data_2
```

```{r}
data_3
```

## `bind_rows()`

When two tibbles have the **same columns** but **different
information**, they can be **merged by "stacking them up" one on top of
the other**. This can be done with the help of the *verb* `bind_rows()`.
If we use it within a pipeline, the left-hand side of the pipe will be
placed on top of the right-hand side argument.

For instance, the datasets `data_1` and `data_2` have the same column
names, but different information (values for `id` and `var_1`). Hence,
we can merge them with `bind_rows()`

```{r}
data_1 %>% 
  bind_rows(data_2)
```

As you can see, the values of `data_1` are on top of the values of
`data_2`. Success!

## `bind_cols()`

If, on the other hand, two datasets **share the same row names** but
**different columns** it is sometimes useful to merge them by
**"attaching" their columns with the *verb*`bind_cols()`**.

For example, `data_3` contains the same id's as `data_1`. Thus, we could
be interested in attaching the values of the columns `var_2` and `var_3`
to have a more complete dataset.

```{r}
data_1 %>% 
  bind_cols(select(data_3, starts_with("var")))
```

Success! ... or is it?

There are two drawbacks when using `bind_cols()`:

1.  **It does not verify the conformity of the rows**. For instance, a
    simple permutation in one of the datasets or the lack of conformity
    in terms of rows will entail problems.

Suppose that the data in `data_3` is slightly reordered. For simplicity,
we've ordered in the descending order of `id`

```{r}
data_3 <- data_3 %>% arrange(desc(id))
```

Carrying the merge with `bind_cols()` will yield an inconsistent result!

```{r}
data_1 %>% 
  bind_cols(select(data_3, starts_with("var")))
```

That doesn't look so good!

2.  The tibbles you want to merge **must have the same number of rows**.

To illustrate what happens, suppose we want to merge our three datasets
to have all the information in one tibble. The first two can be merged
using `bind_rows()`, yet, when we attempt (wrongly!) to merge (the
permutated!) `data_3`, we encounter error messages.

```{r, error=TRUE}
data_1 %>% 
  bind_rows(data_2) %>% 
  bind_cols(data_3)
```

## `left_join()`

A safer procedure to merge two tibbles sharing common elements is to use
the `*_join` verbs of `{dplyr}`. There is a variety of these functions,
but we will use the `left_join()` verb, which merges two datasets
according to their common elements.

In the animation below, we have two datasets, `x` and `y`. A call to
`left_join()` has the particularity that, other than joining the common
elements, it also **preserves the non-shared elements of the first
tibble**, i.e. the *left-hand side* tibble.

![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gadenbuie/tidyexplain/master/images/left-join.gif)

**Source:** [Garrick Aden-Buie's](https://twitter.com/grrrck) Tidy
Animated Verbs

By default, the join is performed using all the columns shared by the
datasets, but one can specify a subset of columns to join with the `by`
argument.

Let's try joining our three datasets using the common column `id` as the
joining key.

```{r}
data_1 %>% 
  bind_rows(data_2) %>% 
  left_join(data_3, by = c("id"))
```

No more errors. Moreover, all our problems with `bind_cols()` are gone.
Namely, the join is robust against permutations in the data because it
relies upon the joining *key* column, i.e. it ensures that there is
consistency in the values of `id` and its respective rows in each of the
datasets.

As a final remark, notice that the common values of the joining *key*
that are preserved are those in the tibble that comes in the
**left**-hand side of the pipeline. As the illustration shows, joining
when there's an `id` that is not in `data_1` has for effect loss of that
information.

Let's illustrate this by adding a supplementary observation with `id=8`
(not present in `data_1`) to the `data_3` dataset and creating the
tibble `data_4`.

```{r}
data_4 <- bind_rows(data_3, tibble(id = 8, var_2 = 3, var_3 = 12)) 
data_4
```

When applying `left_join()`, we obtain

```{r}
data_1 %>% 
  left_join(data_4, by = c("id"))
```

# Pivoting Data

When distributed in tables, data can come in two ways:

-   **long** format, where all columns denote columns. These are useful
    for analysis and the construction of visualisations.
-   **wide** format, where some columns are named after values of a
    categorical column. They are mostly used to display tables in your
    reports.

```{r ,echo = FALSE, fig.cap='Wide-format, vs. Long-format data', fig.align='center', out.width = "80%"}
  knitr::include_graphics("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gadenbuie/tidyexplain/master/images/static/png/original-dfs-tidy.png")
```

To pivot a table, i.e. transform a table from *wide* format into *long*
or vice- versa, we use two functions of the package `{tidyr}`:
`pivot_longer()` and `pivot_wider()`.

```{r ,echo = FALSE, fig.cap='The brooms of `{tidyr}` will help us tidy our data!', fig.align='center', out.width = "30%"}
  knitr::include_graphics(
    path = str_glue("https://d33wubrfki0l68.cloudfront.net/\\
                    476fa4025501dcec05be08248b32d390dd2337d5/\\
                    574c6/css/images/hex/\\
                    tidyr.png")
    )
```

In the animation below, we can overview how pivoting works.

![](https://fromthebottomoftheheap.net/assets/img/posts/tidyr-longer-wider.gif)

Source: [Garrick Aden-Buie's]() Tidy Animated Verbs modified by [Mara
Averick](https://twitter.com/dataandme)

## `pivot_longer()`

Pivot longer has three main arguments:

|  Argument   | Use                                                                                        |
|:-----------------------------------:|:---------------------------------|
|   `cols`    | the **columns to convert** into a single column                                            |
| `names_to`  | the **name of a new column** where we the **names of the selected columns** will be stored |
| `values_to` | the **name of the column** where we will store **the values**                              |

This case scenario can arrive when we have **many measurements carried
through time**. For instance, the makeshift table `data_wide` contains
observations of the performance of a series of prototypes observed at
three timepoints: `t_1`, `t_2`, `t_3`

```{r}
data_5_wide <- 
  tibble(
    prototype = 1:5 ,
    t_1 = c(12,1,3,4,5),
    t_2 = c(13,0,3,6,3),
    t_3 = c(14,-1,3,8,1))
data_5_wide
```

For visualisation or analysis purposes, it would be helpful to *pivot*
this tibble in a long form. Let's use the arguments of the function, as
in

```{r}
data_5_long <- 
  data_5_wide %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -c(prototype),
    names_to = "timepoint", 
    values_to = "measure"
  )

data_5_long
```

This procedure has multiplied the rows in the dataset. We can add a
couple of (optional) arguments

```{r}
data_5_long <- 
  data_5_wide %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -c(prototype),
    names_to = "timepoint", 
    values_to = "measure", 
    names_prefix = "t_", # to remove the `t_` prefix
    names_transform = list(timepoint = as.integer) # to transform 
  )

data_5_long
```

**Long-form tibbles are practical to perform computations and
visualisations**. For instance, we could compute the average measure for
a given prototype from this tibble, (which is a harder task in a
Wide-form tibble!)

```{r}
data_5_long %>% 
  group_by(prototype) %>% 
  summarise(average_measure = mean(measure))
```

## `pivot_wider()`

In a way, `pivot_wider()` performs the opposite operation as
`pivot_longer()`. The idea is to "*spread*" the values of a column and
put them as column names (or columns).

Other than the `data`, which can be inserted via a `pipe`, its main
arguments are:

|   Argument    | Use                                                                            |
|:-----------------------------------:|:---------------------------------|
| `names_from`  | the columns whose contents will become the names of the new columns            |
| `values_from` | the column from which the function will *fetch* the values for the new columns |

While not practical for computations, Wide-form tibbles are useful for
**presentation** purposes, especially in written reports! For
illustration, let's see the following (makeshift) example. Imagine that
you're presented with a table containing the average yields of a series
of crops according to various types of agricultural practices.

```{r}
data_6_long <- 
  tibble(
    crop = c(rep("wheat", 3), rep("corn", 3), rep("quinoa",3)), 
    practice = rep(c("Type 1", "Type 2", "Type 3"), 3), 
    yield = c(12,65,85,98, 65, 45, 72, 67, 59)
    )
data_6_long    
         
```

This does not look very succinct for presentation in a written report
due to the repetition of the values in columns `crop` and `practice`.
Using `pivot_wider` and taking the column names from the `practice` and
the values from `yield` makes for a more succinct table.

```{r}
data_6_long %>% 
  pivot_wider(names_from = practice, values_from = yield) 
```

This table is presentation-ready! We can pass it to `kable()` and take
advantage of `{kableExtra}` to have an even better rendering.

```{r}
library(kableExtra)
data_6_long %>% 
  pivot_wider(names_from = practice, values_from = yield) %>% 
  kbl(caption = "Table 1: Yields of crops according to agricultural practices") %>%
  kable_classic(full_width = F, html_font = "Cambria")
```
